results.title: Evidence-calibrated Dependency Exposure beyond Package Presence
results.abstract: Software composition analysis often begins with package identity and version. That fact is necessary but insufficient: an affected dependency may be absent from the deployed artifact, the affected region may be missing, a discovered call path may be infeasible, or attacker-controlled data may not reach the relevant state. SHADOWDEP defines a scoped evidence model that separates eight predicates from resolution through bounded effect confirmation. The unit is an immutable application, artifact, dependency, vulnerability, configuration, and principal tuple. Missing evidence remains unknown; a negative conclusion requires a scoped refutation certificate. The accompanying artifact implements a versioned policy, schema, 38 semantic controls, and deterministic synthetic validation. Across 200,000 synthetic objects, all 65,536 four-valued evidence states and 1,235,260 metamorphic transformations satisfied the registered invariants. In the registered generator, binary reachability reduced review by 57.49 percent but falsely refuted 18.15 percent of actionable exposures. Conservative reachability reduced review by 42.48 percent at 0.52 percent false refutation. SHADOWDEP reduced review by 75.01 percent at 0.95 percent, with 94.82 percent high-priority precision. These values validate policy behavior under explicit synthetic assumptions only; no real-project exposure rate or named-tool performance is claimed.

results.title: AI-Induced Supply-Chain Compromise: A Systematic Review of Package Hallucinations and Slopsquatting Attacks
results.abstract: Abstract The adoption of large language models (LLMs) and AI‑assisted programming has accelerated software production, but it has also created a novel supply‑chain vulnerability: package hallucination. When an LLM generates code, it may recommend nonexistent third‑party packages that “sound” plausible. Adversaries can register these phantom names in public registries, thereby poisoning the open‑source software supply chain. This attack pattern, termed \textit{slopsquatting}, combines aspects of typosquatting and dependency confusion but is triggered by AI hallucinations rather than human error. We systematically review this emerging threat. Following PRISMA‑2020 guidelines, we searched IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, SpringerLink, Scopus and arXiv for publications (2018–Oct 2025) on package hallucination, typosquatting, dependency confusion, supply‑chain compromise and registry policies. Twenty‑one peer‑reviewed papers and seven credible industry reports met the inclusion criteria. We synthesize definitions, threat models and observed incidents; report empirical evidence of hallucination prevalence across LLMs (e.g., GPT‑series models hallucinate 5.2 \% of packages versus 21.7 \% for open‑source models); and map defenses at IDE, registry, CI/CD and runtime layers. We compare slopsquatting with typosquatting and dependency confusion using a new taxonomy and highlight gaps in current safeguards. Official policies from npm, PyPI, Maven Central, RubyGems, NuGet and CRAN show varying levels of name reservation, deletion and immutability. Our review exposes an urgent need for package‑existence validation within AI coding tools, stricter registry name policies and standardized provenance attestations.

results.title: Should we welcome hallucinated references?: citation integrity beyond fabricated sources
results.abstract: The phenomenon of hallucinated references, non‑existent publications invented by generative AI tools that seem plausible, has prompted understandable concern in scholarly publishing. I argue that the prevailing response is too myopic. Hallucinated references present a serious research integrity problem, but they are also a particularly visible manifestation of a broader citation pathology that is the use of real references to support claims that the cited works do not in fact establish. The latter problem is harder to detect because it cannot be resolved by checking whether a bibliographic item exists, requiring instead semantic judgement about the relation between a citing claim and a cited source. I argue that the current scandal should therefore be used to widen, rather than narrow, editorial concern with reference integrity. The existing infrastructure and tools already address parts of this problem, from metadata checking to citation‑context classification, but they do not remove the need for institutional responsibility. Thus, the response to the current crisis should aim at accountability for citation practices, rather than merely better detection of fabricated sources.
